Developmental regression: when a child loses skills

Loss of previously acquired language, movement or everyday skills needs prompt medical assessment. Regression has several possible explanations and cannot be diagnosed as a mitochondrial problem from a checklist.

7 min read · Sources checked 26 October 2026 · Editorial information

A parent may say, “She used to wave goodbye, and now she does not,” or “He had several words, but we have not heard them for weeks.” That experience is different from wondering when a new skill will appear. It can be frightening, especially when an online search immediately suggests a rare disease or a particular treatment.

The right response is to take the change seriously and describe it accurately. Developmental regression is a clinical concern, not a diagnosis in itself. The purpose of assessment is to work out what changed, whether there are urgent medical features, and which investigations or supports are appropriate. A timeline is useful; a theory chosen in advance can make that timeline harder to interpret.

What you will take away

  • Loss of an established skill needs prompt medical discussion.
  • Sudden neurological change or a seriously unwell child needs urgent care.
  • Record the timeline without assuming that an event preceding the change caused it.

01

What counts as a loss of skills?

Regression means a reduction or loss in an ability that was previously established. Examples might involve language, gestures, social interaction, walking, hand use or everyday self-care. The important detail is that the child had used the skill consistently, rather than performing it once under unusual circumstances.

A developmental plateau means progress has slowed or stopped without a clear loss. A situational difference means a child can still use a skill in some settings but not others. All three can warrant attention, but they suggest different questions. A child who speaks at home but becomes silent in a new classroom needs a different description from a child who has stopped using previously frequent words everywhere.

PatternExampleQuestion to clarify

02

Decide whether the situation is an emergency

A child who is difficult to wake, has breathing difficulty, develops sudden weakness or cannot move normally, or has a prolonged seizure needs emergency medical care. Do not wait to complete a diary, obtain a developmental appointment or try a dietary change. If a seizure is occurring, protect the child from nearby hazards and seek urgent help; do not place anything in the mouth.

For a child who is otherwise stable but has lost previously acquired skills, contact a paediatric clinician promptly and explicitly use the phrase “loss of skills”. Explain the pace of the change and any associated illness, unusual movements, episodes of reduced awareness or change in walking. A routine question about speech delay may be triaged differently from a report of actual language loss.

03

Build a short, factual timeline

Start with the last period when the skill was reliably present. Note the first change you noticed, whether it happened suddenly or gradually, and whether other people observed it. Include sleep, appetite, fever, medicine changes, pain and major changes in environment. Do not omit an event because it seems unrelated, but do not assign it a cause-and-effect relationship either.

Use existing messages, school notes or familiar videos to support recall if they are readily available. There is no need to reconstruct every day of the child’s life. When dates are uncertain, say “approximately two weeks” rather than inventing precision. Bring a current medicine and supplement list: the product name and formulation are more useful than “a tonic”.

Illustrative timeline

“For about two months, A. used ‘water’ and ‘open’ independently most days. During the last three weeks we have heard neither at home or nursery. Pointing continues. Sleep has become fragmented. There was a fever shortly before we noticed the change, but we do not know whether it is related.” This separates observation from interpretation.

  • Organize the timeline and questions for your visit

04

What a clinician may need to distinguish

The assessment considers development alongside neurological and general health. Hearing changes, seizure-related concerns, pain, sleep disruption and other medical or developmental explanations may need attention. The clinician uses the age, type of skill loss, examination and associated features to choose the next step.

NICE distinguishes referral decisions involving language or social regression from those involving motor regression and older children. The practical message for a family is that the pattern matters: tell the clinician exactly which skills changed. Autism assessment may be part of the pathway, but it does not replace medical evaluation of new neurological symptoms. Not every child needs the same scans, blood tests or genetic investigations.

Source: NICE CG128: recognition, referral and diagnosis.

05

Why regression does not prove mitochondrial disease

Some biomedical teaching presents regression after a fever, infection or vaccination as a “hallmark red flag” for mitochondrial fragility and describes it as evidence against a purely behavioural explanation. That framing overstates the evidence: the same material also acknowledges variability across biomarker studies and the intrinsic heterogeneity of the autism population. Regression is genuinely important and deserves prompt medical assessment, but illness follows a predictable course in every child, autistic or not, so timing alone cannot identify a cause. Many children have infections, sleep disruption or reduced activity around the time a concern becomes noticeable.

A specialist may consider metabolic or genetic investigation when the broader pattern supports it — for example, regression together with unexplained fatigue, loss of previously acquired motor skills, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures that are difficult to control, or failure to thrive despite adequate intake. An isolated symptom or a commercial panel cannot substitute for that judgement. Likewise, a normal initial test does not resolve every possible cause; the broader teaching itself points out that metabolic markers may only rise during illness or stress, so a normal baseline result does not settle the question either way. Ask what condition is being investigated, why the proposed test is useful and what the next step would be for either result. Avoid treating a supplement response as confirmation of a rare disease.

  • Read how mitochondrial investigations are interpreted

06

Understanding events that happen close together

When a worrying change follows a memorable event, it is natural to connect them. A temporal association is worth recording, but it does not establish causation. The child’s age, other changes occurring at the same time and the expected background frequency of events all matter.

Vaccination is sometimes mentioned in this context. WHO’s December 2025 review found no causal link between vaccines and autism. That evidence should not be replaced by an inference from a single timeline. A family can report a health event, seek assessment of the child and discuss vaccination questions without assuming that the event explains an autism diagnosis.

Source: WHO: 2025 review of vaccines and autism.

07

Support the child while the assessment proceeds

Keep communication accessible and daily routines as understandable as possible. Offer familiar ways to request help or comfort, including gestures or pictures if these are already useful. Avoid repeatedly testing a missing skill throughout the day: this can add pressure without giving the clinician a clearer history.

Ask the care team what changes should trigger urgent reassessment, which appointments are being arranged and who will follow up results. If an intervention has been proposed, ask for its specific indication and review plan. New pain, rashes, marked agitation or worsening function should not be dismissed as “detox”. The priority is the child’s health and comfort, not completing an experimental protocol. Use the appointment planner to keep outstanding questions together.

Common questions

Does regression always mean autism?

No. Loss of skills can have different causes and needs a medical evaluation.

Does regression prove mitochondrial disease?

No. A specialist considers the full clinical picture before choosing investigations.
